title: Why Circuits Need Memory
excerpt: Every gate you've built so far forgets everything the instant its inputs change. Here's the one trick that lets a circuit remember.

content.text: Every circuit you've built up to this point,  half adders, multiplexers, majority voters,  shares one property: its outputs depend only on its current inputs. Feed a half adder the same A and B twice, ten seconds apart or ten years apart, and you get the exact same SUM and CARRY both times. There's nothing in the circuit that could possibly know or care what happened a moment ago.

That category of circuit has a name: combinational logic. It's everything you've studied so far, and it's genuinely most of what digital logic is. But it can't do a few things that every real computer needs to do,  count, hold a running total, remember which state a machine is in, store a byte after the input that produced it is long gone. All of that needs a circuit whose output depends on more than just its current inputs. It needs history. It needs

Take any purely combinational circuit,  say, an AND gate feeding a NOT gate. At every instant, its output is a pure function of its inputs at that same instant. Change an input, and after one propagation delay, the output updates and that's the whole story. There is no way to look at that circuit's current output and learn anything about what its inputs used to be. The moment an input changes, the old value is gone,  not stored somewhere and inaccessible, just genuinely nowhere in the circuit anymore.

That's fine for an adder. It's useless for a light switch that should stay on after you let go of the button, a counter that should keep counting after the clock tick that incremented it has passed, or a single bit of RAM. All three of those need a circuit that can hold a value independent of what its inputs are doing right now.

body.text: The Trick: Feed a Gate's Output Back Into Itself

content.text: Every circuit you've wired so far has flowed one direction: inputs on the left, gates in the middle, outputs on the right, no wire ever looping back upstream. Sequential logic breaks that rule on purpose. Take a gate's output and route it back around into one of its own inputs (or a neighboring gate's input, which loops back into it), and something new happens: the gate's output is no longer just a function of its external inputs. It's now also a function of what it was already outputting a moment ago, because that old output is literally one of the things feeding it right now.

That's the entire idea behind every sequential element you'll meet in this section, the SR latch, the gated D latch, the D flip-flop. Different wiring, different rules for when the stored value updates, but every single one is built from ordinary combinational gates (NAND, NOR, and friends) arranged with a feedback path. There's no special "memory gate" primitive hiding underneath,  it's the exact same gates you already know, just connected in a loop instead of a straight line.

It's worth saying explicitly why this isn't a problem the way an infinite loop in a program would be: a feedback loop in a digital circuit isn't recomputing forever, it's settling. Each gate has a small propagation delay, so a signal chasing itself around a loop reaches a steady, self-consistent value and then stops changing, the same way a value can stabilize after a few passes of relaxation in any iterative system.

The rest of this section builds up one storage element at a time, in the order real digital design courses teach them, because each one directly fixes a problem with the one before it. First, the SR latch: two cross-coupled gates, the simplest possible feedback loop that stores a bit,  and one very real problem it can't avoid. Then the gated D latch, which fixes that problem by trading two inputs for one. Then the D flip-flop, which fixes a different, subtler problem by changing
the stored value is allowed to update at all. By the end, you'll know exactly what a real register is built from and why it's built that way, not just that it exists.
